children.title: Dental Crowns in McLean, VA
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

children.title: Protect and restore a weak, cracked or worn tooth
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html: A dental crown is a tooth-shaped cap that covers a damaged tooth to protect it and restore its shape and strength. Crowns are used for cracked, weak or worn teeth, after a root canal, and on top of dental implants. Placing one usually takes two visits a few weeks apart, and crowns last five to 15 years on average with good care. At our McLean office, crowns are one of the areas of focus for Dr. Mehdi S. Adili, DDS, a prosthodontist.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

content.tpl: [[@nodes:children]]

children.title: What a Dental Crown Does
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html:
A crown covers the whole visible part of a tooth, down to the gumline. It holds a weakened tooth together, protects it from breaking further, and gives it back a normal shape so you can chew comfortably.

Crowns are a restorative treatment first, but they also change how a tooth looks: a tooth-colored crown can cover a badly stained or misshapen tooth. When a tooth is too damaged for a filling but can still be saved, it may need an inlay, an onlay or a crown, depending on how much healthy tooth is left.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

content.tpl: [[@nodes:children]]

children.title: When You Might Need a Crown
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html: Cleveland Clinic lists these common reasons for a crown. Your exam and X-rays show which applies to your tooth.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

image.alt: Ideal Dental Solutions team member at the McLean office

children.tpl: [[@img:image]]
[[@nodes:children]]

items.title: A Weak or Heavily Filled Tooth

content.title: When decay or an old filling has left too little healthy tooth, a crown can strengthen what remains so it does not break.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: A Cracked Tooth

content.title: A crown holds the pieces of a cracked tooth together and protects it from cracking further.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: After a Root Canal

content.title: Back teeth treated with a root canal usually need a crown to protect them. We handle the root canal and the final restoration in the same office.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: A Worn-Down Tooth

content.title: Teeth worn down by grinding or wear can be rebuilt to their normal height and shape with crowns.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: On Top of a Dental Implant

content.title: A single tooth implant is finished with a custom crown that sits on the implant.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: To Hold a Bridge

content.title: A traditional dental bridge is held by crowns on the teeth on either side of a gap.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

children.tpl: [[@items:items]]

body.html: Request an appointment to find out whether a crown is right for your tooth.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]
[[@nodes:children]]
[[@nodes:children]]

content.tpl: [[@nodes:children]]

children.title: Crown Materials Compared
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html: Crowns come in several materials. Each balances looks, strength and how much tooth has to be reshaped.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

image.alt: Dental model of the upper and lower teeth

children.tpl: [[@img:image]]
[[@nodes:children]]

items.title: All-Ceramic or Porcelain

content.title: Looks the most like natural enamel, so it is a common choice for front teeth. It is also an option for people with metal allergies.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: Zirconia

content.title: A very strong ceramic that can withstand heavier biting forces than other ceramic crowns.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: Porcelain-Fused-to-Metal

content.title: Combines the strength of metal with a tooth-colored porcelain surface. Over time the porcelain can chip and show the metal underneath.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: Metal (Gold or Alloy)

content.title: Rarely chips or breaks and needs only a small amount of enamel removed. The metal color is the main drawback, so it is mostly used for back teeth.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: Resin

content.title: Usually less expensive, but more fragile and more likely to break than porcelain-fused-to-metal crowns. Temporary crowns are often made of resin.
content.tpl: [[@text:title]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

children.tpl: [[@items:items]]

body.html: We will recommend a material for your tooth and explain why, based on where it is, how you bite and how it should look.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]
[[@nodes:children]]
[[@nodes:children]]

content.tpl: [[@nodes:children]]

children.title: What to Expect: Usually Two Visits
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html:
First visit. We examine the tooth and take X-rays. The area is numbed, and some enamel is removed so the crown can fit over the tooth. Then we take an impression, either with a putty-like material or with a handheld digital scanner, and place a temporary crown.

While the crown is made. A dental lab usually takes two to three weeks to make the final crown. The temporary crown protects your tooth in the meantime; avoid sticky and hard foods on that side.

Second visit. We check the shape, color and fit of the new crown, then bond it to your tooth with dental cement and adjust your bite.

Most people go back to work or school right after. Some sensitivity for a couple of weeks and gum soreness for a few days are normal.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

content.tpl: [[@nodes:children]]

children.title: How Long Crowns Last and How to Care for Them
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html:
According to Cleveland Clinic, the average dental crown lasts five to 15 years, and some last much longer with good care. To help yours last:

  • Brush at least twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste and a soft-bristled toothbrush.
  • Floss between your teeth once a day.
  • Avoid chewing ice and very hard, crunchy or sticky foods.
  • If you grind your teeth, ask about a custom night guard.
  • Keep up with regular cleanings and exams.

Call us if a crown feels loose, chips or cracks, or if your bite feels off after it is placed.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

content.tpl: [[@nodes:children]]

children.title: Your Crown Dentist in McLean
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html:
Dr. Mehdi S. Adili, DDS, is a prosthodontist: a dentist with three to four additional years of specialty training in restoring and replacing teeth with crowns, bridges, dentures and implants. He earned his Doctor of Dental Surgery degree from Georgetown University and completed his prosthodontics training at Virginia Commonwealth University. His areas of focus include crowns, bridges, complete dentures, dental implants and full-mouth restoration.

Our office is at 8280 Greensboro Drive, Unit 105, in McLean, close to Tysons.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

content.tpl: [[@nodes:children]]

children.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Dental Crowns
children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html: Answers to the questions we hear most about crowns. For advice about your own tooth, start with an exam.

children.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

items.title: How long does a dental crown last?

body.html: Five to 15 years on average, according to Cleveland Clinic, and some last much longer with good care. Brushing, flossing, avoiding very hard foods and regular checkups all help.

content.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: Does getting a crown hurt?

body.html: The tooth is numbed before it is shaped, and you can ask for more anesthetic if you feel anything. Some sensitivity for a couple of weeks and gum soreness for a few days afterward are normal.

content.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: How many visits does a crown take?

body.html: Usually two. At the first visit we shape the tooth, take an impression and place a temporary crown. The final crown is bonded at the second visit, typically two to three weeks later.

content.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: Do I need a crown or a filling?

body.html: A filling repairs a smaller area of decay. A crown is used when too little healthy tooth is left for a filling to hold, when the tooth is cracked, or after a root canal on a back tooth. Your exam and X-rays decide.

content.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: What should I do if my crown feels loose or comes off?

body.html: Call our office. Keep the crown if it came off, avoid chewing on that side, and we will see whether it can be cemented back or needs to be replaced.

content.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

items.title: Can a crown go on a dental implant?

body.html: Yes. A single tooth implant is finished with a custom crown that attaches to the implant. Implant crowns are cared for much like natural teeth.

content.tpl: [[@rich:body]]

items.tpl:
[[@text:title]]
[[@nodes:content]]

[[@nodes:children]]

children.tpl: [[@text:title]]

body.html: Have a cracked, worn or weak tooth? Call (703) 442-0442 or request an appointment, and we will look at the tooth and explain your options.

documents.title: Teeth Grinding at Night: Signs, Causes and When a Night Guard Helps
documents.seoTitle: Teeth Grinding at Night and Night Guards | Ideal Dental Solutions
documents.description: Grinding your teeth at night? The signs, common causes, what a custom night guard does and does not do, and when to see a dentist in McLean, VA.

facts.label: Common signs
facts.value: Worn or chipped teeth, sore jaw, morning headaches

facts.label: Linked with
facts.value: Stress, sleep apnea, smoking, alcohol and caffeine

facts.label: Custom night guard
facts.value: Can last several years with care

documents.answer: Grinding or clenching your teeth, called bruxism, usually happens during sleep, so many people do not know they do it. Common signs are worn, chipped or cracked teeth, a sore jaw and dull morning headaches. A custom night guard from your dentist does not cure grinding, but it protects your teeth from the wear and damage it causes. If you notice these signs, or a partner hears you grinding, have a dentist take a look.

sections.heading: What teeth grinding is
sections.html:
Bruxism means clenching, grinding or gnashing your teeth. It happens in two ways:

  • Sleep bruxism happens at night. The American Dental Association notes that most people who grind do it while they sleep, which is why many do not realize it.
  • Awake bruxism happens during the day, often when you are tense, worried or concentrating.

Cleveland Clinic notes that grinding in your sleep can cause more harm than clenching during the day, and that people who only clench while awake may not need treatment beyond becoming aware of the habit.

sections.heading: Signs you might be grinding
sections.html:
Because sleep grinding happens unnoticed, a dentist often spots it first. Signs to watch for include:

  • Teeth that look worn, flattened, chipped or cracked, especially along the edges
  • A sore or tired jaw, especially in the morning
  • Dull headaches or facial pain when you wake up
  • Earaches or neck pain
  • Pain when eating, or trouble opening and closing your mouth
  • A partner or family member hearing grinding at night

sections.heading: What causes it
sections.html:
Cleveland Clinic says there is no single known cause; several factors play a part. The most common ones are:

  • Stress and anxiety. Grinding is often linked to feeling tense or overwhelmed.
  • Sleep problems. Research shows a link between sleep apnea and grinding, though it is not clear which causes which.
  • Smoking, alcohol and caffeine. According to the ADA, people who smoke or drink alcohol or coffee are twice as likely to grind their teeth.
  • Some medications, including certain antidepressants (SSRIs).
  • Teeth that do not line up, or missing or crooked teeth, which the ADA lists among possible causes.

If you snore, stop breathing for moments at night or wake up tired, mention it. A sleep study may help find the cause.

sections.heading: Why grinding is worth treating
sections.html: Over time, grinding can wear down enamel, chip or crack teeth and damage fillings, crowns and other dental work. Cleveland Clinic also lists TMJ disorders, facial pain and sleep problems among the possible effects of untreated grinding. Protecting your teeth early can help you avoid bigger repairs, like crowns, later on.

sections.heading: How a night guard helps
sections.html:
A night guard is a thin, removable appliance worn over your teeth while you sleep. It takes much of the force of grinding, which helps protect your teeth. It does not make the habit go away.

Custom or store-bought? The ADA says a custom guard made from a mold of your teeth gives the closest, most comfortable fit, and that store-bought guards may not give the same protection. Cleveland Clinic adds that a guard that does not fit well can make your teeth, gums or jaw sore. A sports mouthguard is a different kind of guard, made to protect your teeth during sports.

At Ideal Dental Solutions, we make custom night guards from hard acrylic, designed from a digital scan of your teeth. Bring it to your regular visits so we can check the fit and condition.

sections.heading: Other ways to reduce grinding
sections.html:
• Manage stress. The ADA mentions meditation, counseling, exercise, massage and deep breathing.
  • Cut back on caffeine and alcohol, and if you smoke, quitting helps.
  • Notice daytime clenching. Mayo Clinic suggests resting your tongue up, with your teeth apart and your lips closed.
  • Ask about other treatments. For some people, a doctor may suggest a muscle relaxant at bedtime for a short time, or, when other treatments have not helped, injections that relax the jaw muscles.

sections.heading: Caring for your night guard
sections.html: Cleveland Clinic recommends rinsing your guard in cool water after each use, cleaning it with a brush and soapy water, letting it air dry and keeping it away from heat, which can warp it. Store it in its case, and bring it to your dental checkups so we can check it for cracks and wear. With care, a custom night guard can last several years.

sections.heading: Grinding, jaw pain and TMJ
sections.html: Grinding and clenching can strain the jaw muscles and joints. If you have jaw pain, clicking with pain, or trouble opening your mouth, see us for an exam. The NIH's National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research recommends starting with conservative, reversible care for jaw joint and muscle problems, and advises against a splint or guard designed to change your bite for good. Learn more about our TMJ and TMD treatment.

cta.heading: Think you might be grinding?
cta.text: Book an exam at our McLean office. We will check your teeth and jaw for signs of grinding and, if it helps, fit you for a custom night guard.

faq.q: Do I need a night guard if I only clench my teeth?
faq.a: Possibly. Clenching during sleep can wear and stress teeth just like grinding. If you only clench while awake, becoming aware of the habit may be enough. An exam shows whether your teeth are being damaged.

faq.q: Will a night guard stop me from grinding?
faq.a: Not usually. A night guard protects your teeth from the force of grinding. Managing stress, sleep problems and habits like caffeine, alcohol and smoking can help reduce the grinding itself.

faq.q: Are store-bought night guards good enough?
faq.a: They cost less, but the ADA and Cleveland Clinic both say they may not protect as well as a custom guard, and a poor fit can make your teeth, gums or jaw sore.

faq.q: How long does a custom night guard last?
faq.a: With proper care, a custom night guard can last several years. Bring it to your checkups so we can look for cracks, wear or changes in fit.

faq.q: My child grinds their teeth. Should I worry?
faq.a: Children often grind their teeth, and the ADA notes that many outgrow it by adolescence. Mention it at your child's next dental visit so the dentist can check for wear.
